main.text: The number of the unclean birds, and their general marks. How their prohibition pertained to morals.

Now that we have tried to set out the roll of the unclean birds, we shall add something about their number and marks from Maimonides' book On Forbidden Foods. These are the words of chapter 1, section 14: סימני עוף טהור לא נתפרש מן התורה אלא מנה מינין טמאין בלבד ושאר מיני העוף מותרין והמינין האסורין ארבעה ועשרים הן ואלו הן א נשר ב פרס ג עזניה ד׳ דאה והיא הראה האמורה במשנה תורה ה׳ איה והיא הדייה האמורה במשנה תורה ו׳ מין האיה שכן כתוב בה למינה מכלל שהיא שני מינין ז עורב ח זרזיר שכן נאמר בעורב למינו להביא את הזרזיר ט׳ יענה י׳ תחמס יא׳ שחף יב׳ נץ יג׳ ושרנקא והיא מין הנץ שכן כתוב בו למינהו יד׳ כוס טו׳ שלך יו׳ ינשוף יז׳ תכשמת יח׳ קאת יט׳ רחמה כ׳ חסידה כא׳ האנפה כב׳ מין האנפה שכן נאמר בה למינה כג׳ הדוכיפת כד׳ העטלף, The signs of the clean birds are not explained in the Law, which only drew up a roll of the unclean ones, and the remaining species are permitted. The prohibited species, moreover, are twenty-four. 1. NESER. 2. PERES. 3. OZNIIA. 4. DAA, which in Deuteronomy is called RAA. 5. AIA, which in Deuteronomy is called DAIA. 6. A species of the AIA [tēs]; because of it is written after its kind: so it is a genus with two species. 7. OREB. 8. ZARZIR; because of OREB it is said after its kind, to designate ZARZIR. 9. IAANA. 10. THACHMAS. 11. SACHAPH. 12. NETS. 13. And SARNEKA, which is a species of NETS; because of it is written after its kind. 14. CHOS. 15. SALACH. 16. IANSUPH. 17. THINSEMETH. 18. KAATH. 19. RACHAMA. 20. HASIDA. 21. ANAPHA. 22. A second species of ANAPHA; because of it is said after its kind. 23. DU- [col. 353] KIPHATH. 24. ATALLEPH.

In this roll of Maimonides some things should be noted. First, that דאה daa and ראה raa are rightly taken as the same. For anyone comparing Leviticus with Deuteronomy it will be plain that one was written for the other, because of the similarity of the letters Daleth and Res. R. Abja rightly observes this in the Talmudic tractate Cholin, fol. 63 a–b. But it is not equally true, as these same writers would have it, that איה aja and דיה daja are the same, and that the bird called איה aja in Leviticus is called דיה daja in Deuteronomy. That, I say, is not true, since in Deut. XIV, 13. both are found, האיה והדיה, as distinct birds. Indeed both names also occur outside the Law: namely איה in Iob. XXVIII, 7. and דיות [III, 120] in Es. XXXIV, 15. Accordingly we have distinguished them: for us איה aja was the merlin (aesalon) ^{a)}, and דיה daja the black vulture ^{b)}.

Second, from the fact that Moses prohibits certain birds after its kind, it does not follow that there are different species of them. For he did not say in the plural, after their kinds, but in the singular, after its kind: evidently to signify that the whole species is prohibited. And what he says expressly in some cases, he was content to have supplied in others, so as to avoid the tedium of constantly repeating these words, after its kind.

Third, I do not understand why the Hebrews want זרזיר zarzir, that is, the starling, to be a species of raven rather than the crow, or the magpie, or the jackdaw and daw, which come closer to the nature of the raven. Yet Maimonides does not bring this forward on his own account. For the Aruch cites it thus from the tractate Cholin, fol. 63: זה עורב למינה להביא את הזרזירין, this raven is said to be after its kind in order to designate the zarzirin (or starlings). There, however, I do not find the word הזרזירין, or of the starlings, today. But in Bava Kama fol. 92 b one may read a proverb that arose from it, which runs thus: לא לחנם הלך זרזיר אצל עורב אלא מפני שהוא מינו, not in vain does the starling go to the raven, since it is of the same species. And in Beresith Rabba ch. 65, somewhat more briefly: לא הלך זרזיר אצל עורב אלא שהוא מינו, The starling would not go to the raven unless it were ὁμογενής [homogenēs]. And in Baal Hatturim the Cabalists observe that the words עורב למינו, the raven after its kind, by Gematria have the same value as זרזיר zarzir. For in Hebrew numerals each is worth 414. And in Aquinas זרזיר zarzir is defined as עוף שהוא קרוב לצורת העורב, a bird that is similar in form to the raven. Nor is there any doubt that זרזיר zarzir is the starling. For in the Gloss on the Talmud it is explained as אשטו״רניל estournel. And in Pomarius, storno. And in Masal Kadmoni, Fable 51, the two interlocutors are called in Hebrew השפן והזרזיר, that is, the rabbit and the starling, as appears from the picture. Finally, the Arabic زرزور [zarzūr] zarzour means the very same thing. Accordingly, the words of Dioscorides in book 2, in the chapter On the Dung of Animals, ψαρὰς ὀρύζῃ τρέφοντες [psaras oryzē trephontes], feeding starlings on rice, Avicenna, in book 2 of the Canon, in the chapter زبل [zibl], that is, On Dung, rendered thus: الزرزور المتعلف للارز [al-zarzūr al-mutaʿallif lil-aruzz] Zarzur fed on rice: that is, the starling, not the thrush, as the Latin translators rendered it, by an error that arose in Spain, where zorzal is the thrush.

Less familiar is the word שרנקא sarneka, which Maimonides uses for a species of נץ nets, or hawk, as the Talmudists use שורינקא sorinka and, what is the same, בר־חיריא bar-chirja. The words run thus in the tractate Cholin, in the place cited above: הנץ ה״ר [III, 121] זה הנץ למינהו להביא את בר־חיריא מאי בר־חיריא אמר אביי שורינקא Our masters have handed down that the hawk is said to be after its kind so that bar-chirja may be signified. What is bar-chirja? Abji said: It is forinka. The Aruch reads [col. 354] בר־חוריא bar-churja, and שורניקא sornika. And in Arabic, in Giggeius, سرنوق [surnūq] surnouk is a bird of the hawk kind, living by prey. Either I am mistaken, or this is the same bird that Damir in one copy calls شروق [shurūq] saruk, in another زرق [zurraq] zurrak: of which Ibno-Saida says thus: طاير يصاد به بين البازي والباشق [ṭāyir yuṣād bihi bayna al-bāzī wa-al-bāshiq] It is a bird used in fowling, intermediate (that is, of intermediate size) between Albazi and Albasak, species of hawk very well known among the Arabs. And Alphera: هو البازي الابيض والجمع الزرارق وهو صنف من البازي لطيف الا ان مزجه احر وايبس ولذلك هو اشد جناحا واسرع طيرانا واقوي اقداما وفيه ختل وخبث وخير الوانه الاسود الظهر الابيض الصدر الاحمر العين [huwa al-bāzī al-abyaḍ wa-al-jamʿ al-zarāriq wa-huwa ṣinf min al-bāzī laṭīf illā anna mizājahu aḥarr wa-aybas wa-li-dhālika huwa ashadd janāḥan wa-asraʿ ṭayarānan wa-aqwā aqdāman wa-fīhi khatl wa-khubth wa-khayr alwānihi al-aswad al-ẓahr al-abyaḍ al-ṣadr al-aḥmar al-ʿayn] It is Albazi (or the white hawk). The plural is zerariko. It is an elegant species of hawk, but of a very hot and very dry temperament. And therefore it is stronger in its wings, swifter in flight, and stronger in its feet. And there is in it cunning, and malice, and excellence of colour. For it is black on the back, white on the breast, red in the eye. From the whiteness of its breast it is called by the Talmudists בר־חוריא, son of whiteness. It should be examined whether it is the white falcon of the moderns.

These are the names of the unclean birds, both those that are read in Scripture and those that the masters of the Jews put forward from tradition. To draw up a list of them was easy for Maimonides; but he did not even attempt what we expected from such a teacher, to interpret them. And, what is more surprising, the Talmudic doctors, who are so many centuries older, explain only a few, and those very ambiguously, so that they plainly grope in sheer darkness. The Greek translators too, who lived as long before most of the Talmudists as these did before Maimonides, often got stuck here, as is shown by how little they agree with themselves and by how they pull the name of a single bird into such different meanings. In the Babylonian captivity, of course, the Jews partly forgot their own language, and the purity of Hebrew degenerated into Syriac. Hence, after the return from that captivity, the true meaning of some words that were rarely used was lost. Among these were certain names of birds. Hence Aben Ezra on Levit. XI, 29. 30., where Moses forbids eight kinds of creeping things, says: גם אלה השמנה לא נוכל לדעתם גם העופות כי אם מדברי קבלה, We cannot truly know either these eight (creeping things) or the birds, except from the words of tradition. But this tradition is nowhere extant. And the Talmudists, the authors of the traditions, refer us elsewhere, namely to skilled fowlers. Thus in [III, 122] Cholin fol. 63. b.: א״ר יצחק עוף טהור יאכל במסורת נאמן הצייד לומר עוף זה טהור מסר לי רבי א״ר יוחנן והוא שבקי בהן ובשמותיהן, R. Isaac said: A clean bird is eaten on the tradition of a trustworthy fowler, so that you may say: This bird is clean, as my master (a fowler) handed down to me. R. Iochanan: Provided he is experienced in them and in their names. Hence Maimonides, in the place cited above, section 15: כל מי שהוא בקי במינין אלו ובשמותיהן הז״ אוכל כל עוף שאינו מהם ואינו צריך בריקה ועוף טהור נאכל במסורת והוא שיהיה דבר פשוט באותו מקום שזה [col. 355] עוף טהור ונאמן צייד לומר עוף זה התיר לי רבי הצייד והוא שיוחזק אותו צייד שהוא בקי במינין אלו ובשמותיהן Whoever is practised in those species (which are forbidden) and in their names freely eats all the birds that are not in that list, and needs no further investigation. And a clean bird is eaten on the basis of tradition, when this is clearly stated in the place where the clean bird is found; and there a fowler is trustworthy, so that (the one who eats) may say: My master the fowler permitted this bird to me. That is, provided the fowler is established as practised in them and in their names. But since fowlers of this kind are nowhere to be found, he adds in section 16: מי שאינו מכירן ואינו יודע שמותיהן בודק בסימנין אלו שנתנו חכמים כל עוף שהוא דורס ואוכל בידוע שהוא מאלו המינין וטמא ושאינו דורס ואוכל אם יש בו אחד משלשה סימנין אלו הז״ עוף טהור ואלו הן אצבע יתירה או זקף והיא המוראה או שהיה קרקבנו נקלף ביד Whoever does not know those birds and does not know their names distinguishes them by these signs, which the sages have handed down to us. Every bird that tears its prey by trampling on it and devours it is plainly of those species and is held unclean. But a bird that is not rapacious and carnivorous is held clean if one of these three signs is found in it. Namely, 1. if it has a superfluous toe (that is, a spur, such as cocks have); 2. or a crop, which in Hebrew is called murea; 3. or if its gizzard can be stripped by hand (without a knife). These are taken partly from the Talmudic tractate Cholin, partly from the Chaldee paraphrase of Jonathan, which reads thus at Levit. XI, 13.: וית אלין מיניא תשקצון מן עופא דלית להון ציבעא יתירא ודלית זקפתא ודקורקבניה ליתוהי מקליף, And these species of birds you shall abhor: those which have no superfluous toe, and which have no crop, and whose gizzard is not stripped. This last I do not quite understand. Yet the Geonim make so much of this last sign that, if this one alone is lacking in a bird, they never permit it to be eaten, as Maimonides explains at length. But whoever is curious about trifles of this kind should consult the cooks of the Jews.

The reason for these prohibitions seems to have been wholly mystical. 1. God forbade the birds of prey, namely the eagle, the ossifrage, the kite, the vulture, the hawk, the raven, etc., in order to turn the Jews away from robbery. 2. The nocturnal birds, namely the eagle owl, the little owl and the bat, so that they might cast off the works of darkness and show themselves children of light. 3. The birds of lakes and riverbanks, such as the onocrotalus, the catarrhactes, the pelican and the stork, [III, 123] whose food is most impure, and the hoopoe, which nests in dung, so as to keep them from all uncleanness. 4. Finally the ostrich, which does not rise from the ground, so that, leaving earthly things behind, they might strive toward the things that are above. This explanation is not ours but that of the ancient interpreters. Aristeas: Περὶ ὧν δὲ ἀπηγόρευται πτηνῶν, εὑρήσεις ἄγριά τε, καὶ σαρκοφάγα, καὶ καταδυναστεύοντα τῇ περὶ ταῦτα δυνάμει τὰ λοιπά· [Peri hōn de apēgoreutai ptēnōn, heurēseis agria te, kai sarkophaga, kai katadynasteuonta tē peri tauta dynamei ta loipa] As for the birds that are forbidden, you will find that they are wild and carnivorous, and by their strength exercise tyranny over the others. Barnabas at once transfers this to morals in the Epistle which our eminent Vossius edited: Οὐδὲ μὴ φάγῃς, φησὶ, τὸν ἀετὸν, οὐδὲ τὸν ὀξύπτερον, οὐδὲ τὸν ἰκτῖνα, οὐδὲ τὸν κόρακα· οὐ μὴ, φησὶ, κολληθήσῃ ἀνθρώποις τοιούτοις, οἵ τινες οὐκ οἴδασι διὰ κόπου καὶ ἱδρῶτος πορίζειν ἑαυτοῖς τὴν τροφὴν, ἀλλ' ἁρπάζουσι τὰ ἀλλότρια ἐν ἀνομίᾳ αὐτῶν· [Oude mē phagēs, phēsi, ton aeton, oude ton oxypteron, oude ton iktina, oude ton koraka; ou mē, phēsi, kollēthēsē anthrōpois toioutois, hoi tines ouk oidasi dia kopou kai hidrōtos porizein heautois tēn trophēn, all' harpazousi ta allotria en anomia autōn] Nor shall you eat, he says, the eagle, or the hawk, or the raven: that is, you shall not join yourself to those who do not know how to earn their living by toil and sweat, but seize what belongs to others through their iniquity. Clement of Alexandria, not content with having quoted this in book 5 of the Stromata, also imitates it thus in the Paedagogus, book 3, chapter 11: Οὐδ' ἰκτῖνα, ἢ ὠκύπτερον μαστοφαγῆ, ἢ [col. 356] ἀετὸν φάγῃς, φησίν· οὐκ ἐγγιεῖς, φησὶν, τοῖς δι' ἁπαγῆς τὸν βίον πορίζομένοις· [Oud' iktina, ē ōkypteron mastophagē, ē aeton phagēs, phēsin; ouk engieis, phēsin, tois di' hapagēs ton bion porizomenois] You shall not eat the kite, or the hawk that devours breasts, or the eagle: that is, do not approach those who obtain their living by plunder. Origen, in Homily 7 on Leviticus, says: You shall not eat these, because they are unclean: the eagle, and the vulture, and the rest like them. For these birds always feed on dead bodies, and live off dead carcasses. All, therefore, who lead a life of this kind are to be held unclean. I think that those too are named in these who brood over the deaths of others, etc., as if gaping after the carcasses of the dead. In the same place he also asserts that those who in their words display heavenly learning, yet in their deeds perform carnal and dead works, are rightly called vultures and eagles, which swoop down from the heights upon dead and stinking flesh. And a little later: Some love not so much rapacity as obscurity and darkness. For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, like little owls and bats, etc. Novatian, On Jewish Foods, chapter 3: Who (would make food of) the raven? But he execrates crafty dispositions. When he forbids the sparrow (he meant στρουθὸν [strouthon], that is, the ostrich), he rebukes intemperance. When the little owl, he hates those who flee the light of truth. When the swan, the proud with lofty neck. When the charadrius, the excessively chattering intemperance of the tongue. When the bat, those who seek the darkness of night and of error alike. In Cyril, book 9 Against Julian, eagles, hawks, catarrhactae, griffins and vultures signify the rapacious and greedy; the raven, the shifty; the hoopoe, little owl and bat, the ignorant and lovers of darkness, who hate the light of doctrine. And in book 14 On Adoration the same author has much more on the same subject. There too he counts not only the hoopoe but also the heron and the charadrius [III, 124] among the nocturnal birds together with the little owl and the bat, asserting that γλαῦκα, καὶ ἐρωδιὸν, καὶ χαραδριὸν, καὶ τὰ ὅμοια αὐτοῦ, ἐπόπα, καὶ νυκτερίδα [glauka, kai erōdion, kai charadrion, kai ta homoia autou, epopa, kai nykterida], the little owl, and the heron, and the charadrius, and those like them, the hoopoe and the bat, are rejected as νυκτὸς φίλα, καὶ χαίροντα μὲν τῷ σκότει, καὶ πτήσει ὡς ἡδυτάτην ἐν αὐτῷ ποιεῖσθαι μεμελετηκότα, κατεχθραίνοντα δὲ τὸ ἡλίου φῶς, καὶ τὸ ἐν αὐτῷ τι δρᾷν μὴ ἀνεχόμενα [nyktos phila, kai chaironta men tō skotei, kai ptēsei hōs hēdytatēn en autō poieisthai memeletēkota, katechthrainonta de to hēliou phōs, kai to en autō ti dran mē anechomena], birds that are friends of the night, delight in darkness, and are accustomed to fly more gladly in it, and that shrink from the light of the sun and cannot bear to undertake anything in it. This indeed fits the little owl and the bat, but not the hoopoe, the heron and the charadrius. Yet Procopius of Gaza follows Cyril on this point in his Commentaries on Leviticus. But in matters pertaining to nature the sacred doctors are not always to be trusted, since cares of greater moment did not allow them to devote serious attention to these trifles.

Above all I like the acumen of Thomas, who, following the version and order of Jerome, transfers something from each of these birds to morals. "In the eagle," he says ^{c)}, "which flies high, pride is forbidden. In the gryphon, which is hostile to horses and men, the cruelty of the powerful is forbidden. In the haliaeetus, which feeds on small birds, those are signified who harass the poor. In the kite, which makes the greatest use of ambushes, the deceitful are signified. In the vulture, which follows an army, waiting to eat the corpses of the dead, those are signified who strive after the deaths and seditions of men, so as to profit from them." Read the passage, and you will see that he pursues the rest with equal care. Yet he does so in such a way that he reports certain things about the birds that are not quite true: 1. for instance, that the porphyrio has one foot broad for swimming and the other split for walking; that the herodio (that is, the ardea [heron]) is the same as the falcon; that the caladrius (that is, the charadrius) is a garrulous bird, etc. He also has some ἀποδόσεις [apodoseis] that are forced and extorted by violence, which was the malady of those times. Nevertheless, in many places the talent of that man shines forth, worthy of a better age.
